I am 39 years old and I have been farming these 5 mu in Quzhou County for 20 years, since I was 19. I finished middle school, and two years ago I went to a village training where an extension worker talked about new wheat varieties and fertilizer. But honestly, I mostly trust what I see with my own eyes and what my neighbors do. My household has 5 people. My husband and my sister-in-law work in a garment factory in the county town and send money back, so I do most of the farm work myself, with help from my mother-in-law and my daughter during busy times.

My land is split into three pieces. The biggest piece, 2.5 mu, I keep for wheat and maize rotation — that is my main food crop. The second piece is 1.5 mu of cotton for cash income. The last piece is 1 mu of peanuts on the sandy corner of my field, also for cash and for oil at home.

For the winter wheat on those 2.5 mu, I will sow in early October. I use Jimai 26, which is an improved variety. My neighbor Aunt Li used it and got over 1000 jin per mu last year, so I switched to it three years ago and it works well. For each mu, I put down one bag — 50 kilograms — of 16-16-16 compound fertilizer as base fertilizer. That gives me about 8 kilograms each of nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium per mu. Then at green-up time in March, I top-dress with 20 kilograms of urea per mu, which is another 9 kilograms of nitrogen. So in total that is about 17 kilograms of nitrogen, 7 kilograms of phosphorus, and 7 kilograms of potassium per mu. I will irrigate three times: the winter irrigation in November to keep the seedlings from freezing, once at jointing stage in late March, and once at grain filling in mid-May. I spray pesticide twice — once in spring for aphids, once before heading for powdery mildew. I plough the field before sowing the wheat, turning the soil over after the maize residue is cleared. I expect about 500 kilograms per mu if the weather is normal.

For the summer maize on that same 2.5 mu, I plant right after wheat harvest in early June. There is no time to plough — everyone here does no-tillage direct seeding after the wheat straw is chopped. I use Zhengdan 958, a hybrid variety. I put 40 kilograms of 15-15-15 compound fertilizer per mu in the row at sowing. Then at the big trumpet stage in July, I spread 15 kilograms of urea per mu. That comes to about 14 kilograms of nitrogen, 6 kilograms of phosphorus, and 6 kilograms of potassium per mu. I irrigate twice: once right after sowing if the soil is dry, and once at tasseling in late July. Two sprays for armyworm and corn borer. If things go well, I can get 550 kilograms per mu.

For cotton, I have 1.5 mu. I plant in late April. I use hybrid cotton seeds — I buy 2 kilograms of seed per mu from the dealer. I spread one 50-kilogram bag of 16-16-16 compound fertilizer per mu as base, and I also put some chicken manure from my yard on the field because cotton likes fertile soil. Then I top-dress twice with urea: 15 kilograms at flowering and 10 kilograms at boll stage. Cotton uses a lot of potassium, so I add an extra 10 kilograms of potassium chloride per mu. Total nutrients are about 15 kilograms nitrogen, 7 kilograms phosphorus, and 8 kilograms potassium per mu. I irrigate three times — at flowering, at peak boll, and in August if it is dry. I spray pesticide five times because bollworm and aphids will destroy everything if you are lazy. I do rotary tillage in spring to break up the soil. I expect about 250 kilograms of seed cotton per mu.

For peanut on my 1 mu, I plant in late April or early May. Peanuts do not need much nitrogen because they fix their own, so I only use 40 kilograms of 15-15-15 compound fertilizer per mu at planting. That is about 6 kilograms nitrogen, 6 kilograms phosphorus, and 6 kilograms potassium per mu. I might add a small 20-kilogram bag of calcium fertilizer if I have extra money after buying the wheat fertilizer, because peanuts need calcium for the pods. I irrigate twice: once at flowering and once at pod filling. Three pesticide sprays for leaf spot and aphids. Rotary tillage in spring. I expect about 300 kilograms of pods per mu.

Why these amounts? Because last year this is what I applied, and I did not lose money. My neighbor Lao Wang tried to save money on cotton fertilizer last year — he cut back by one bag per mu — and his yield dropped by nearly 100 kilograms per mu. He lost much more than he saved. I would rather spend an extra 50 yuan per mu on fertilizer than risk a bad harvest. A bad harvest means my daughter's school fees are in trouble. Wasting some fertilizer is just a cost; losing yield is a disaster. I also watch what the big farmers around me do. If everyone is applying similar amounts, then I know the market price and the soil conditions support it. With my husband working off-farm, we have cash to buy inputs, but I still calculate everything carefully. A bag of urea is about 100 yuan now, and compound fertilizer is 150 yuan per bag. For my 5 mu, I will spend about 1,800 yuan on chemical fertilizer this year. That is a lot, but I have to do it.
